canonical_policy.name: Correctness and clarity before optimization
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Prefer clear correct code first; do not introduce specialized optimizations without a concrete reason and prefer measurement/profiling for non-trivial optimization.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Clear-first and workload evidence requirement covered, including preoptimization query investigation; replica0095 explicitly retains verifying material improvement.

context_quotes:
Prefer clear, correct code first. Do not introduce specialized performance
optimizations without a concrete reason; for non-trivial optimizations, prefer
measurement or profiling evidence over assumptions.

By default, introduce these only for a measured or clearly demonstrated need:
`EF.CompileQuery`/`EF.CompileAsyncQuery`, `ValueTask<T>`,
`ArrayPool<T>`/`MemoryPool<T>`, manual object pooling, custom serialization
optimizations, aggressive caching, and raw SQL for performance. Do not sacrifice
maintainability for speculative micro-optimization.

Do not prematurely optimize normal Angular code. Use route lazy loading and
sensible rendering and data access first; introduce memoization, virtual
scrolling, custom change-detection work, or other optimizations after
identifying a real need.

Report performance concerns only when credible, for example obvious N+1
database access, unbounded materialization, repeated expensive external calls,
blocking asynchronous I/O, or heavy allocation in a demonstrated hot path. Do
not recommend caching, compiled queries, pooling, `ValueTask`, or similar
optimizations speculatively.

Copy only repository-level build files that exist and are required by restore.
Copy project files required for restore explicitly; avoid fragile wildcard

## Restore Caching

Copy project and build dependency files before the full source tree so source
changes do not invalidate NuGet restore layers. Update the project-copy section
when the solution structure changes; do not optimize caching at the cost of a
Dockerfile that no longer restores the actual project graph.

Start with clear LINQ and optimize after identifying a real problem. Before
specialized optimization, inspect the number of round trips, selected columns,
N+1 behavior, indexes, generated SQL, the query plan where necessary, the amount
of data materialized, and tracking overhead.

`Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, stack allocation, and pooling are performance
tools. Use ordinary arrays, strings, and collections by default.

## Serialization

Prefer `System.Net.Http.Json` / `System.Text.Json` where sufficient. Use
explicit serialization options when the external contract differs from the
application's defaults, and do not reuse internal Domain entities as remote API
contracts merely to avoid mapping.

Constructing `new HttpClient(testHandler)` in a focused test is fine; the
lifetime rule concerns production code.

adding resilience pipelines without understanding their behavior.

canonical_policy.name: Database access is efficient by default
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Filter/project in the database when practical, avoid unnecessary round trips/over-fetching/N+1 patterns, and paginate potentially large result sets.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Database shaping and intentional tracking/DTO exception covered by EXTRA0122..0124. Existing U0008/U0009 preserve LINQ-specific needs/keyset recommendation, not new.

context_quotes:
Keep database work efficient by default: filter and project in the database
when practical, avoid unnecessary round trips, over-fetching, and N+1 query
patterns, and paginate potentially large result sets. EF Core technique:
`ef-core` skill.

For read-only queries that need only selected data, prefer database-side
projection.

Projection is not mandatory when the use case genuinely needs the entity, but
avoid loading a complete aggregate only to return two scalar fields.

Use tracking intentionally: normal tracking queries when loaded entities will be
modified and committed through the current Unit of Work; `AsNoTracking()` for
read-only entity queries where change tracking provides no value. Do not add
`AsNoTracking()` mechanically to projections that already produce non-entity
DTOs.

## Primary-Key Lookups

`FindAsync` fits when querying by primary key, an entity instance is required,
and returning an already tracked entity is desirable:

```csharp
var order = await db.Orders.FindAsync(
    [orderId],
    cancellationToken);
```

Use LINQ when additional predicates, projection, related data, or query shaping
are required.

## Related Data

Prefer an explicit query shape: projection when only selected related data is
needed; `Include`/`ThenInclude` when the entity graph itself is required. Avoid
lazy loading by default because it hides database access and causes N+1
queries. For large collection includes, consider split queries and verify the
generated SQL and performance.

Apply filtering, ordering, and pagination in the database, and always use
deterministic ordering for paged queries:

Avoid loading all rows and filtering in memory when the database can filter,
lazy loading by default, fire-and-forget EF asynchronous operations, and raw SQL
introduced merely to appear more performant.

| Scenario | Default technique |
|---|---|
| Read-only entity query | `AsNoTracking()` when useful |
| Read model | Database-side projection |
| Primary-key entity lookup | `FindAsync` when its semantics fit |
| Complex entity graph | Explicit `Include` / projection |
| Set-based mass update/delete | `ExecuteUpdateAsync` / `ExecuteDeleteAsync` when appropriate |
| Normal query | Ordinary LINQ |
| Measured extremely hot query | Consider a compiled query |
| Multiple commits requiring atomicity | Explicit transaction |
| Production schema change | Reviewed migration script, controlled deployment |
| Empty Development database | Run the maintained development seeder |
| Need a fresh local seed dataset | Recreate the local database explicitly |

## Transactions

A single `SaveChangesAsync` is normally the transaction boundary for one
application operation. Use an explicit transaction when a concrete use case
needs several database operations or several `SaveChangesAsync` calls to succeed
atomically. Do not attempt distributed transactions with EF transaction APIs.

## Compiled Queries

Normal LINQ is the default; EF Core already caches query compilation by query
shape. `EF.CompileQuery`/`EF.CompileAsyncQuery` pay off only on a measured hot
path where profiling shows compilation or cache lookup overhead is material — not
merely because a query runs frequently.

Start with clear LINQ and optimize after identifying a real problem. Before
specialized optimization, inspect the number of round trips, selected columns,
N+1 behavior, indexes, generated SQL, the query plan where necessary, the amount
of data materialized, and tracking overhead.

Use raw SQL only when EF Core cannot express the query effectively or measured
performance justifies it, and prefer EF APIs that preserve parameterization
(`FromSql`, `FromSqlInterpolated`, `SqlQuery`) over string-built SQL.

Avoid loading all rows and filtering in memory when the database can filter,
lazy loading by default, fire-and-forget EF asynchronous operations, and raw SQL
introduced merely to appear more performant.

Normal structured `ILogger` logging is sufficient for most code. For measured
high-volume logging hot paths, consider source-generated `LoggerMessage` APIs
(example in `references/serilog.md`); do not add them everywhere to avoid
theoretical allocations.

| Scenario | Default |
|---|---|
| Application logging API | `ILogger<T>` |
| Context shared across logs | `BeginScope` |
| Unexpected handled exception | Log once at the handling boundary |
| Expected business rejection | No Error log |
| Serilog setup, sinks, enrichers | `references/serilog.md` |
| High-volume measured hot path | Consider `LoggerMessage` |

Raw string literals do not make raw SQL appropriate by themselves.
